title: CausalRAG2: Hierarchical Knowledge Graphs for Truthful Reasoning
one_liner: A retrieval system that organizes knowledge into causal-gated modules so the AI can skip across distant evidence without chasing spurious dead ends.
lead: When you ask a large language model a complex question with multiple facts scattered across your documents, today's systems often get lost. They either stay trapped in one neighborhood of related facts (missing evidence far away), or they pull in misleading connections (spurious correlations). CausalRAG2 solves this by organizing knowledge into semantic neighborhoods and then adding explicit causal gates — shortcuts that let retrieval jump across neighborhoods only when it makes logical sense. The result: faster answers because fewer irrelevant facts are retrieved, and more accurate answers because the retrieved facts are causally tied to the real answer rather than spotted by accident.

problem.h2: Knowledge graphs trap retrieval in one room
paras: When your knowledge base grows large, facts naturally cluster: all machine-learning papers together, all physics papers together, and so on. A naive retrieval system starts with a seed fact (the part of the question it understands), then walks outward in a circle, collecting nearby facts. This works fine if all the evidence you need is in one cluster.

But complex questions span clusters. A question like 'Which scientist won the Nobel Prize for work in thermodynamics?' needs evidence from the physics cluster (who studied thermodynamics) and the Nobel Prize cluster (who actually won it). If your retrieval starts in physics, it circles through physics-related facts endlessly and never jumps to the Nobel cluster. This is the information isolation problem: you miss distant evidence entirely.

The other trap is spurious correlation. A naive system sees 'temperature' mentioned near 'Nobelprize-ceremony-videos' and thinks they are connected, even though one is about physics and one is about award ceremonies. The retrieved context gets polluted with red herrings, and the language model's answer becomes unreliable.

callout.html: CausalRAG2 adds causal gates: explicit shortcuts that skip across disconnected clusters only when there is a real cause-and-effect link, suppressing spurious paths and reaching distant evidence reliably.

paras: Most graph-based retrieval systems treat the knowledge graph as a flat collection of entities and edges. CausalRAG2 reorganizes that graph into a two-level structure: base entities at the bottom, and semantic clusters (modules) above, with explicit causal gates connecting clusters. This hierarchical organization enables the rest because once you name each module's semantic identity and test causal links between them, you can weight traversals intelligently (preferring causal bridges) and suppress spurious local loops.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Causal gate strength
hidden.name: causal gate strength
paras: Every pair of modules has a causal gate: a binary flag (0 or 1) indicating whether a real cause-and-effect link exists between them. This is not visible in the raw knowledge graph; you have to infer it by asking the language model 'Do these two topics logically connect?' The strength is simple: either there is a gate (1) or there is not (0).

During retrieval, high-strength gates (confirmed causal links) are weighted heavily (weight 1.2), encouraging the model to traverse across them. Spurious connections (no causal gate) are suppressed, forcing retrieval to stay local unless a real bridge exists. The paper estimates causal gates by feeding module-pair descriptions to the language model and decoding a yes/no prediction.

heat.caption: Darker means causal gate (strong logical link). Highlights show links the paper identifies as real bridges.

reads.html: A causal gate is a yes/no marker that says 'these two clusters of facts are genuinely related by cause and effect, not just coincidence.' The paper's language model learns to spot real bridges and ignore false connections.

CausalRAG2 constructs causal gates via LLM-based pairwise verification (LLM-EstCausal) across module pairs. Gates are undirected and binary, enabling shortcuts that bypass modular boundaries while suppressing spurious correlations.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Causal gates rescue distant evidence
paras: The root problem is modularity. When a knowledge graph has 100+ clusters, and your evidence is in a cluster far from where the query started, naive traversal circles locally and never reaches it. CausalRAG2 solves this by asking: which distant clusters are actually relevant? A cause-and-effect relationship is your answer. A physicist's work connects to the Nobel Prize because one causes or enables the other. A physicist's work does not logically connect to random weather data.

Once causal gates are built (an offline step), online retrieval is simple: start from seed entities (matched to the query), walk outward in N hops using both local edges and causal gates as shortcuts, but weight causal gates higher (1.2) so the model prefers real bridges over generic structure. Because gates are sparse and targeted, you skip isolated noise. Because they are causal (verified by the language model), you land on evidence that actually answers the question.

The final filter matters most: after retrieval brings in candidate facts, the language model re-checks each one to remove spurious correlations ('Does this fact actually explain the answer, or is it just mentioned nearby?'). This two-stage filtering — gate-guided traversal plus causal re-verification — breaks the hold of information isolation and noise simultaneously.

stages.s: Traverse N hops using causal gates as bridges
Filter: language model re-verifies causal relevance
Clean context subgraph grounded in distant evidence

math.words: Traversal weight = 1.2 if causal gate exists, 1.0 if hierarchical edge, 0.8 if generic structural edge. Prefer causal bridges by multiplying path score by accumulated edge weights.
math.equation: path_score = product of (w_i) for each edge i, where w_i in {1.2, 1.0, 0.8} depending on edge type
symbols: how confident the retrieval is in a traversal path
multiply all edge weights together along the path

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Path A: Start (physics module) -> Generic edge to thermodynamics (0.8) -> Causal gate to Nobel cluster (1.2) -> Result entity (1.0). Score = 0.8 × 1.2 × 1.0 = 0.96.
Path B: Start (physics) -> Generic edge to unrelated weather data (0.8) -> No causal gate (path blocked). Score = 0.0.
Path C: Start (physics) -> Hierarchy edge to physics-submodule (1.0) -> Causal gate to Nobel (1.2) -> Prize entity (1.0). Score = 1.0 × 1.2 × 1.0 = 1.2.
Path C wins: the model prefers traversals that use causal gates, and reaches the Nobel Prize evidence reliably.

math.note: Paths that use causal gates accumulate higher scores, so retrieval naturally prefers real bridges over spurious local loops.

bars.h2: How causal gates reduce noise and reach distant facts

charts.title: Flat graph-based retrieval
charts.note: Naive traversal brings back many entities but mostly local clusters, misses distant answers, and mixes in noise.

charts.title: CausalRAG2 with causal gates
charts.note: Causal gates enable jumps across modules to reach distant evidence because the language model has pre-verified that real cause-and-effect links exist between those modules; filtering removes spurious noise because retrieved facts are re-checked to confirm they causally explain the answer. Fewer entities but higher quality.

items.html: If the LLM that verifies causal relationships is biased or hallucinating, it may mark unrelated clusters as causally linked. Extra false gates introduce noise, defeating the purpose.

items.b: Hierarchical pruning cuts off relevant gates.
items.html: To save computation, CausalRAG2 uses a top-down pruning strategy that skips some gate verifications if a parent gate already connects two clusters. This can miss real but rare causal bridges between distant sub-clusters.

items.b: Stale knowledge bases confound memorization with retrieval.
items.html: If the knowledge base is old, the pretrained language model may already know parts of the answer from its training data. Retrieved evidence then looks more relevant than it is, hiding poor retrieval quality.

Carefully verify causal gates (e.g., check LLM outputs by hand on a sample), retain cross-cluster gates even if expensive, and use benchmarks that refresh frequently so no memorized facts bias the evaluation.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small knowledge graph with three disconnected clusters: Biology (genes, proteins), Physics (thermodynamics, temperature), and History (Nobel Prize 1911, Marie Curie). Pose multi-hop questions that require jumping clusters: 'Who won the Nobel Prize for discovering radioactivity?' (answer: Marie Curie, connecting physics knowledge to history knowledge). Measure whether the system retrieves both distant clusters and avoids spurious paths. Compare flat graph retrieval (no gates) against CausalRAG2 (with causal gates). Track two metrics: (1) Does retrieval reach the distant history cluster? (2) Does the final answer exclude spurious physics-weather coincidences?
demo.metric_eq: Context recall = number of gold facts retrieved / total gold facts. Answer correctness = 1 if final answer is Marie Curie, 0 otherwise.
demo.closing: The demo must show that causal gates enable jumps to distant clusters while keeping spurious paths out because gates are only traversed when the language model has confirmed a real cause-and-effect link exists, thereby proving that explicit causal reasoning beats naive traversal.
